```kotlin
val core = ConnectionCore.client(quic, tlsClientConfig, KslQuicCrypto, remote, Random, now)
val out = PacketBatch(capacity = 4)
try {
    while (running) {
        val n = core.poll(out, now)
        for (i in 0 until n) send(out.buffer(i), out.length(i), out.address(i)!!)
        val deadline = core.nextTimeoutOrNever()          // TimeMark.NEVER when no timer is armed; nextTimeout() is the nullable form
        val datagram = receiveOrWaitUntil(deadline)       // your socket; returns null when the deadline passed first
        now = clock()
        if (datagram != null) core.handleDatagram(datagram.buffer, datagram.length, datagram.from, Ecn.NotEct, now)
        else if (deadline <= now) core.onTimeout(now)
        while (true) { val event = core.nextEvent() ?: break; handle(event) }
    }
} finally { out.close() }
```

Stream events tell such a loop when to retry instead of polling: `StreamReadable` after new data, an end or a reset;
`StreamWritable` once acknowledgements free send-buffer room after `writeStream` took fewer bytes than offered, or once the
peer's `MAX_STREAM_DATA`/`MAX_DATA` gives credit to data that was waiting; `StreamsAvailable` once `MAX_STREAMS` raises a
limit that refused `openStream`; `StreamFinished` once a stream is done in both directions and retired.

`core` is reached through `QuicConnection.core` too (`@ExperimentalKuicksilverApi`), but it must only be touched from
the endpoint loop that owns it when the connection came from `QuicEndpoint`.

## TLS with Kuicksilver

Kuicksilver's TLS layer (`io.kuicksilver:kuicksilver-tls`) runs TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846; the default, as RFC 9852 asks) and,
when asked, TLS 1.2 under the RFC 9325 profile as narrowed by RFC 10015 (ECDHE and AEAD only) over OpenSSL 3.5 on every Kotlin Multiplatform target. The same configuration object drives QUIC handshakes,
TLS over TCP and the `ktor-network` socket wrapper. The code blocks below compile and run as `GuideSamplesTest`.

### Native library availability

The TLS layer runs on the native library `libksl`, shipped for the platforms listed in the README. An application that
must also run elsewhere (another OS or CPU architecture) checks once at startup and keeps another transport, instead of
catching `KslException` from the first connection:

```kotlin
// guide:tls:availability
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
if (!KslLoader.isAvailable()) fallBackToTcp()   // never throws; the outcome is cached for the process
```

`KslLoader.isAvailable()` and `KslLoader.availability()` are experimental (`@ExperimentalKuicksilverApi`); the latter says why: `NativeAvailability.Unavailable.reason` is
`NoLibraryForPlatform`, `LoadFailed`, `IntegrityMismatch` (the SHA-256 manifest check refused the library) or
`AbiMismatch`, with the original exception as `cause`. The check makes the same single load attempt as
`KslLoader.ensureLoaded()`; after a failure, `ensureLoaded()` throws that same exception without retrying.

On the JVM the library is extracted once into `<java.io.tmpdir>/kuicksilver-native-<user>` (or
`-Dkuicksilver.native.workdir=<dir>`, for a `noexec` temp directory) and verified against the jar's SHA-256 manifest on
every start. The directory must be a real directory that you own and that nobody else can write (the loader applies
`rwx------`); a symbolic link, another owner or permissions that cannot be removed give `IntegrityMismatch`. The file is
kept between runs and shared between JVMs of the same user: its name carries the `ksl` ABI version.

### Configuration

A `TlsConfig` is immutable; build it with the `tlsConfig` DSL. A client needs a server name (its reference identifier)
and a trust configuration; a server needs an identity or an SNI selector.

```kotlin
// guide:tls:client-config
val client = tlsConfig(TlsRole.Client) {
    serverName = "server.test"          // SNI and the name the certificate must match
    alpn = listOf("h2", "http/1.1")
    trust = TrustConfig.Platform        // the OS trust store (JDK, Android NSC, SecTrust, Windows)
}
```

```kotlin
// guide:tls:server-config
val identity = TlsIdentity.fromPem(chainPem, keyPem.toCharArray())   // the key array is zeroed; the key now lives in OpenSSL only
val server = tlsConfig(TlsRole.Server) {
    alpn = listOf("http/1.1")
    this.identity = identity
}
```

#### Rotating the server certificate

A server identity can be replaced while the server runs (experimental, 0.3.0): wrap it with
`TlsIdentity.reloadable(identity)`, use the result as the `identity`, and call `reload(TlsIdentity.fromPem(...))` when a
renewed certificate arrives. Every handshake that starts afterwards, over TCP and QUIC alike, presents the new chain and
key; handshakes in progress and established connections keep the identity they started with, and nothing they hold is
freed under them.

- **Bad input never replaces the identity in use.** A key that does not match the leaf already fails in `fromPem` or
  `fromDer`; `reload` refuses a closed identity, a leaf certificate that has expired, and one that is not valid yet
  (notBefore more than 5 minutes ahead: a certificate staged for later is never served early), all with
  `TlsException.Config`, and the old identity goes on serving.
- **Ownership.** The reloadable identity owns what it serves: `reload` closes the identity it replaces, `close()` the
  current one. An identity `reload` refused is still yours to close.
- **Resumption.** Every server binds its session tickets to the leaf certificate they were issued under, so after a
  reload to another certificate a ticket from before it resumes nothing: the client runs a full handshake and sees the new
  certificate, and that ticket's 0-RTT is refused. A resumed connection carries no certificate (RFC 9846 section 2.2) and
  keeps the identity of its session, which is therefore the current one. After a key compromise, a reload stops both new
  handshakes and resumptions with the old key; connections already established run until they close.

Independently of reloads, resumption is bounded on every server (RFC 9846 section 4.7.1 recommends limiting the total
lifetime of resumption keying material and taking the certificate's lifetime into account): each resumption renews the
ticket, but a chain of renewals ends 7 days after the full handshake that authenticated it (BoringSSL's
`SSL_DEFAULT_SESSION_AUTH_TIMEOUT`) and at the leaf's notAfter; then the client runs a full handshake.

The Ktor server engine can also watch the PEM files itself; see [Certificate rotation](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/ktor.md#certificate-rotation).

### Trust

Host names are always checked (RFC 9525) and the check cannot be disabled; it can be redirected with `ExpectedName`
for proxies (`ExpectedName` wraps `Platform`, `AnchoredCa` or `Custom`; to pin as well, put it inside `Pinned` — except
around `Custom`, which `Pinned` refuses directly and through `ExpectedName`:
`Pinned(pins, base = ExpectedName(name, base))`). Pins are an additional check against the validated chain, never a
replacement for it.

```kotlin
// guide:tls:trust
val pinned = TrustConfig.Pinned(
    pins = setOf(SpkiSha256.parse("sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")),
    scope = PinScope.Leaf,
    base = TrustConfig.AnchoredCa(listOf(rootCertificate)),   // or Platform
)
```

Private CAs usually arrive as PEM files. `Certificate.parsePem` returns every `CERTIFICATE` block of a file in order
(a bundle, a chain), skips other blocks such as keys, and parses each certificate on the spot, so a damaged file fails
at startup with `TlsException.Config` rather than at the first handshake:

```kotlin
// guide:tls:pem-roots
val roots = Certificate.parsePem(caPem)   // every CERTIFICATE block, in order; TlsException.Config if none
val trust = TrustConfig.AnchoredCa(roots)
```

Every certificate given to `AnchoredCa` is a trust anchor, also one that is not self-signed: anchoring at an
intermediate CA accepts the chains that reach it, without its issuers (OpenSSL `X509_V_FLAG_PARTIAL_CHAIN`, as JDK
`TrustAnchor`s, Apple anchor certificates and Go's root pools behave).

#### Platform trust

`TrustConfig.Platform` hands the chain to the platform's own verifier. `ksl` checks the reference identifier with the
shared RFC 9525 matcher afterwards on every platform, so a platform matcher can only make the decision stricter; pins
(`Pinned`) are compared against the chain the platform built, never against certificates the peer merely sent.

Every peer chain is held to OpenSSL's security level 2 (RFC 9325 section 4.5): every key needs 112 security bits (RSA
2048 bits, an elliptic curve 224 bits), and every certificate signature too, except the trust anchor's: no SHA-1 or MD5
(RFC 9846 section 4.5.1.3). A weaker chain ends the handshake with `bad_certificate` and `TlsException.Verify` with
`VerifyReason.WeakKey` or `VerifyReason.WeakSignature`; there is no switch to turn it off. The JDK, Android and Windows
verifiers would accept 1024-bit RSA on their own. Which certificates count depends on the trust:

- **`Platform`** (also under `Pinned` and `ExpectedName`): the platform is asked first, and after its yes `ksl` checks the
  path the platform built, leaf first and its trust anchor last (Android's `X509TrustManagerExtensions`, Apple's
  `SecTrustCopyCertificateChain`, Windows' chain, and on the JVM the path rebuilt with the JDK's PKIX builder to the trust
  manager's roots), as OpenSSL checks its own path: every key, the anchor's included, and every signature but the
  anchor's. A certificate the server sends that the platform does not use, such as an extra cross-certificate above the
  root the platform trusts (signed with SHA-1 by an old root, say), does not count, as with OpenSSL. If the platform does
  not say which path it took, the certificates the server sent are checked as for `Custom`. When the platform itself
  refuses a chain with an MD5, SHA-1 or small-key certificate in it (the JDK, Apple and Windows do), the refusal is still
  reported as `WeakSignature` or `WeakKey` with `bad_certificate`. This holds even when the chain is not trusted at all
  (RFC 9846 section 4.5.1.3 does not depend on trust; OpenSSL would send `unknown_ca`), and it takes precedence over the
  platform's own reason: an expired or revoked chain that also has a weak certificate among those sent is reported as
  `WeakKey` or `WeakSignature`. The chain is refused either way. On Linux Native `Platform` is
  OpenSSL's own verifier with the system store, which checks its own path the same way.
- **`AnchoredCa`**: OpenSSL checks the path it builds to your roots.
- **`Custom` and `Tofu`**: the certificates the peer sent are checked before your verifier or the TOFU store is asked:
  every presented certificate reachable from the leaf through issuers whose key verifies the signature (each such issuer
  is followed, so cross-certificates are all checked), only a really self-signed certificate's own signature exempt. This
  is stricter than OpenSSL for an extra cross-certificate the server sends above the anchor your verifier trusts: it is
  checked and refuses the chain. A certificate on no verified path from the leaf is not looked at.

The endpoint's own chain is held to the same rules when the identity is made (`TlsIdentity.fromDer`, `fromPem` and the
JVM key store factories throw `TlsException.Config` for a SHA-1- or MD5-signed certificate or a key under 112 bits), for
a server and for a client certificate alike.

| Platform | Verifier and store | Revocation |
|---|---|---|
| JVM | the default `X509TrustManager`: the JDK's `cacerts` or `javax.net.ssl.trustStore`, not the OS store | as the JDK is configured (off by default) |
| Android | the platform `TrustManager`, including the app's Network Security Config (whose `cleartextTrafficPermitted` the Ktor client also honours for `http://`) | the platform's policy |
| Apple (macOS, iOS) | `SecTrust` with the SSL policy for the host name: the keychain and the system roots | the platform's policy; an incomplete required check is `UnknownRevocationStatus` |
| Windows (mingwX64) | CryptoAPI: `CertGetCertificateChain` for the `serverAuth` (or, for a client certificate, `clientAuth`) usage with the presented intermediates, then `CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy(CERT_CHAIN_POLICY_SSL)` with the host name: the Windows root store, missing intermediates fetched through AIA | the leaf's status is checked; a revoked leaf is `Revoked`, an unknown status is ignored (soft fail, as browsers); network fetches share a 10 s budget and run off the handshake's thread |
| Linux (Native) | OpenSSL inside `ksl` with the system CA bundle (below) | none |

Windows errors map to `VerifyReason`: `CERT_E_UNTRUSTEDROOT` and chaining failures to `UnknownIssuer`, `CERT_E_EXPIRED` to
`Expired` or `NotYetValid`, `CERT_E_CN_NO_MATCH` to `HostnameMismatch`, `CRYPT_E_REVOKED` and `CERT_E_REVOKED` to `Revoked`,
`CRYPT_E_NO_REVOCATION_CHECK`, `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE` and `CERT_E_REVOCATION_FAILURE` to `UnknownRevocationStatus`,
`CERT_E_WRONG_USAGE` and `CERT_E_PURPOSE` to `InvalidPurpose`, `TRUST_E_CERT_SIGNATURE` to `BadSignature`,
`CERT_E_MALFORMED` to `BadEncoding`; anything else is `UnknownIssuer`.

#### Linux trust store

On Linux Native the bundled OpenSSL has no built-in certificate directory, so `ksl` looks for the system store when a
client context with `TrustConfig.Platform` is built, in this order:

1. `SSL_CERT_FILE` (a PEM bundle) and `SSL_CERT_DIR` (a directory of PEM certificates, hashed with `c_rehash` or not). When
   either variable is set, only these are used, as in Go's `crypto/x509`: a configured store never silently becomes another
   one.
2. Otherwise the first bundle that loads, from Go's list: `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` (Debian, Ubuntu, Gentoo),
   `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` (Fedora, RHEL 6), `/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem` (openSUSE), `/etc/pki/tls/cacert.pem`,
   `/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem` (CentOS, RHEL 7 and later), `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` (Alpine), and
   `/usr/local/etc/openssl/cert.pem`.
3. Otherwise the first of `/etc/ssl/certs` and `/etc/pki/tls/certs` that holds certificates. A directory with `c_rehash`
   links is searched by OpenSSL's hash lookup; any other directory is read like Go reads it: every PEM file in it loads.
   A directory without either does not count.

When nothing is found (a distroless or `scratch` image without `ca-certificates`), building the configuration fails with
`TlsException.Config` naming every path searched:

```text
invalid TLS configuration: ksl: no CA certificates for TrustConfig.Platform; searched /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, ...,
/etc/pki/tls/certs/; install ca-certificates, set SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR, or use AnchoredCa
```

Install the distribution's `ca-certificates` package, copy a bundle into the image and point `SSL_CERT_FILE` at it, or
ship your roots with `TrustConfig.AnchoredCa`.

`TrustConfig.Tofu` stores the first key seen for a name; `TrustConfig.Custom` hands trust to your verifier and still
runs the shared name check afterwards (it is marked `@DelicateKuicksilverApi` for that reason).

### TLS over a socket

```kotlin
// guide:tls:socket
val selector = SelectorManager(Dispatchers.IO)
val socket = aSocket(selector).tcp().connect("server.test", 443).tls(client)
val write = socket.openWriteChannel(autoFlush = true)
val read = socket.openReadChannel()
write.writeStringUtf8("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: server.test\r\n\r\n")
val status = withTimeout(10.seconds) { read.readLine(LineEnding.Lenient) }   // the status line
socket.close()   // sends close_notify, then closes the TCP socket
```

`close()` returns at once and finishes in the background: it sends what is queued and `close_notify`, then closes the
TCP socket. On a client (`Socket.tls`) it drops what is left after 3 s in all (a peer that stopped reading) and closes the
socket anyway; on a server (`Socket.tlsServer`) it waits for the client to take everything, however slowly it reads, so
bound the connection yourself (an idle or stall timeout) where a client may never read.

The same works on the server side with `Socket.tlsServer(config)` after `ServerSocket.accept()`.

#### Resumption and trust

A resumed handshake carries no certificates, so the client checks the chain it cached from the full handshake again
before it offers the ticket (ADR-0011): under `AnchoredCa` and the Linux `Platform` store `ksl` verifies it again
against the trust store, the current time, the name and the purpose; under the other platform verifiers and `Custom`
the verifier runs again on it. Pins are then checked against the cached validated chain. A chain that no longer passes
(an expired leaf, for example) means a full handshake, not a failure. A server holds only the client's leaf of a
resumed session: its verdict travels with the ticket, which resumes only under the same trust configuration and lives
at most `SessionTicketConfig.ticketLifetime`.

### TLS over any channel

`TlsConnection.client(transportIn, transportOut, config)` and `TlsConnection.server(...)` run TLS over any pair of
ktor-io channels, so a TLS session can live inside a QUIC stream or a test harness. `input` and `output` carry
plaintext; `shutdown()` sends what is still queued and `close_notify`, waits for the peer's, and closes after 3 s in
all at the latest, also when the peer stopped reading.

### Key logging

Secrets never leave native memory unless you ask. That includes the TCP client's session cache: a ticket kept for
resumption is a handle to a native OpenSSL session, never its serialized bytes, and the secret is wiped when the
entry is used, replaced, evicted or expires, or when the engine that owns the cache closes. Each Ktor client engine
keeps its own cache of at most 384 sessions, six tickets for each of 64 origins (the least recently stored one is
evicted first); `Socket.tls` and
`TlsConnection.client` share one process-wide cache with the same bound (the cache itself is internal API). `TlsConfig.keylog` accepts a `KeylogSink` (RFC 9850 lines); the
`SSLKEYLOGFILE` variable is not read on the library's own and is ignored by the bundled OpenSSL; only
`keylogFromEnvironment()`, called by the application, turns it into a sink. A `libksl` built against the system
OpenSSL (Linux only, loaded with `-Dkuicksilver.native.path` or `-Dkuicksilver.native.system=true`) refuses to load while
it is set, since that libssl might honour it (`KslException.NativeLoad` "SSLKEYLOGFILE is set and the system libssl may honour it; unset it (keylog)"). `keylogFile(path)` creates the file
with mode 0600 and checks it before the first line: a symlink at the path, a file that is not a regular file, has more than one
hard link or belongs to another user, or a file system without POSIX permissions is refused with an `IllegalArgumentException`, and an existing
file that is readable by the group or others is tightened to 0600 (on the JVM, Linux and Apple). The JVM on Windows has
no POSIX permission view and refuses the file; on Kotlin/Native Windows the file is only created, so keep it in a
directory that only you can write. On the JVM the file is opened once, when the sink is
created, and every line goes through that descriptor, so a file removed and recreated at the path later receives nothing;
the JVM sink is also `java.io.Closeable` (close it when you are done, otherwise the descriptor stays open until the
channel is collected or the process exits). Kotlin/Native reopens the file without following links for every line and
repeats the checks on the new descriptor. A FIFO at the path is refused without waiting for a reader (Native opens with
`O_NONBLOCK`; the JVM checks the path before it opens it), so a planted FIFO cannot stall `keylogFile` or the endpoint loop.

```kotlin
val path = "/tmp/kuicksilver-keys.txt"
// guide:tls:keylog
val debugClient = tlsConfig(TlsRole.Client) {
    serverName = "server.test"
    keylog = keylogFile(path)   // @DelicateKuicksilverApi
}
```

### Key exchange groups

Both roles negotiate TLS 1.3 key exchange from one list: `X25519MLKEM768`, `X25519`, `secp256r1`, `X448`, `secp384r1`,
`secp521r1`. A client sends key shares for the post-quantum hybrid and for X25519, so a server of either kind picks its
group in one flight. A server takes the client's X25519 share when that is all the client sent, even if the client also
lists the hybrid as supported: OpenSSL's default would answer with a HelloRetryRequest for `X25519MLKEM768`, and that
extra round trip doubled the handshake under loss against ngtcp2, picoquic and quiche (interop `handshakeloss`). The
list is not configurable.

## HTTP/3 with Kuicksilver

Kuicksilver's HTTP/3 layer (`io.kuicksilver:kuicksilver-http3`) implements HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) with QPACK (RFC 9204),
extensible priorities (RFC 9218), Extended CONNECT (RFC 9220) and HTTP datagrams (RFC 9297) on top of
`kuicksilver-quic`. Server push is not implemented. The frame and QPACK codecs are sans-IO (ADR-0004); the connection
runtime is a set of coroutines over `QuicConnection` streams. The code blocks below compile and run as
`GuideSamplesTest` (`kuicksilver-http3/src/jvmTest`).

### QPACK

Header compression uses the static table always and the dynamic table only when both sides allow it:

- What we advertise to the peer (`Http3Settings.qpackMaxTableCapacity`, `qpackBlockedStreams`) defaults to 0/0, like
  most implementations: the peer's encoder then sends static references and literals only. `enableQpackDynamicTable()`
  advertises 4096 bytes and 16 blocked streams.
- Our own encoder uses at most `encoderMaxTableCapacity` (4096 by default) of whatever the peer advertises, and blocks
  at most min(peer's `SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS`, 100) streams. Without a blocking budget it still inserts
  entries, but references them only once the peer has acknowledged them.
- At most 1000 sections wait for the peer's acknowledgment; above that the encoder sends static references and
  literals until the peer catches up, so a peer that never acknowledges sections cannot grow the encoder's state.
- `authorization`, `proxy-authorization`, `cookie` and `set-cookie` are never inserted into the dynamic table and are
  sent with the never-index bit (RFC 9204 section 7.1); neither are values longer than a quarter of the table.
- The decoder rejects, before allocating, integers longer than 62 bits and string literals above a ceiling, and counts
  the decoded size of a field section as it goes (name + value + 32 per line, RFC 9114 section 4.2.2), stopping at
  `maxFieldSectionSize`. In a field section the ceiling is `maxFieldSectionSize` itself and a longer string makes the
  section too large (431 on the server, `FieldSectionTooLarge` on the client; the connection lives, RFC 9204 section
  7.4); on the encoder stream it is 64 KiB and a longer string closes the connection with `QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR`.
- An encoder-stream instruction the transport delivers in pieces is reassembled in linear time: once its length is
  known the decoder only appends bytes until it is complete (at most 2 x 64 KiB + 64 bytes are held).
- A field section that references entries still in flight on the peer's encoder stream waits for them (at most
  `qpackBlockedStreams` such streams; one more closes the connection with `QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED`). If the peer
  resets a stream while it waits, the decoder sends a Stream Cancellation.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:qpack
val settings = http3Settings { enableQpackDynamicTable() }   // advertise 4096 bytes / 16 blocked streams
val client = Http3Connection.client(quicConnection, settings)
```

### Messages and errors

Requests and responses are validated as RFC 9114 sections 4.2-4.3 require. A malformed message (a field name that is
not a lowercase token, a control character other than tab in a value (CR, LF and NUL anywhere), whitespace at either end of a value, a connection-specific field such
as `transfer-encoding`, `te` other than `trailers` or `te` in a response, a missing or duplicated pseudo-header,
`:authority` and `host` that disagree or are not `host[:port]`, a classic CONNECT without a port, DATA on a response
to HEAD or with status 204 or 304) is a *stream* error: the stream is reset with `H3_MESSAGE_ERROR` and the connection
keeps serving other requests.

Failures surface as `Http3Exception`:

| Type | When |
|---|---|
| `Http3Exception.Protocol(h3Code, initiator, streamId)` | an HTTP/3 error code closed the connection (`streamId == null`) or reset a stream; unknown codes read as `H3_NO_ERROR` |
| `Http3Exception.Qpack(code)` | a QPACK error (0x200-0x202) |
| `Http3Exception.RequestNotProcessed(retrySafe)` | the server did not process the request (`GOAWAY`, `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED`); safe to retry on a new connection |
| `Http3Exception.MessageError(streamId, reason)` | the peer's message on this stream was malformed |
| `Http3Exception.FieldSectionTooLarge(streamId, limit)` | headers or trailers above `maxFieldSectionSize` once decoded, or above the peer's limit when sending (`streamId` -1: no stream was opened) |
| `Http3Exception.Settings(message)` | an operation needs a setting the peer did not send (Extended CONNECT) |
| `Http3Exception.ConnectRejected(status, headers)` | Extended CONNECT answered with a non-2xx status |

Transport failures stay `QuicException`; `Http3Exception.fromQuic(e)` reads an HTTP/3 meaning out of an application
close or a stream reset. Every exception is copyable (`CopyableThrowable`), and cancellation is never wrapped.

### Endpoints and connections

`Http3Endpoint` binds a QUIC endpoint and speaks HTTP/3 on it. Its TLS configurations must offer ALPN `h3`; a server
closes accepted connections that negotiated anything else. `SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM` follows the transport: it is sent as
1 only when `QuicConfig.maxDatagramFrameSize` is not 0.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:endpoints
val server = Http3Endpoint.bind(
    InetSocketAddress("0.0.0.0", 443),
    QuicEndpointConfig.Builder().apply { this.server = QuicServerConfig.Builder(serverTls /* alpn = listOf("h3") */).build() }.build(),
)
val client = Http3Endpoint.bind(InetSocketAddress("0.0.0.0", 0))
val connection = client.connect(serverAddress, clientTls /* alpn = listOf("h3") */)
```

`Http3Connection.client(quic)` and `Http3Connection.server(quic)` also wrap a `QuicConnection` you already have. Either
way the control stream, the two QPACK streams and SETTINGS go out at once, without waiting for the peer's; a reserved
setting, frame and unidirectional stream are sent too (`Http3Settings.grease`, on by default) so peers stay tolerant of
extensions. The peer's SETTINGS are in `peerSettings` once they arrive. The peer's transport parameters must let us open
those three unidirectional streams (RFC 9114 section 6.2). `server` returns at once and opens them in the background, so
an accept loop never waits on one client; `client` returns once its SETTINGS went out. A peer that does not allow them
within three seconds has its connection closed with `H3_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR` (`client` throws it).

### Client requests

```kotlin
// guide:http3:client-request
val response = connection.request(http3Request("GET", "example.com", "/"))
println(response.status)
val body = response.body            // a ByteReadChannel; reading it to the end completes response.trailers
```

A body ends only with the message: the peer's FIN after its DATA (and trailers, if any), with `content-length`
matched. Then `isClosedForRead` is true and `readAvailable` returns -1. A body cut short — a reset, a connection that
ended, a request abandoned, a frame error — fails every read with its cause (`Http3Exception`, or the
`QuicException.ConnectionLost` of the connection) and is not `isClosedForRead`, so a read loop that stops at -1 never
takes a truncated body for a complete one; `closedCause` says why. The same holds for the request body on the server.

A request body is any `ByteReadChannel`; it is copied into DATA frames as the transport accepts it, so a slow peer
slows the producer instead of filling memory. `trailers` is called after the body ends. Interim responses (1xx,
103 Early Hints included) reach `onInformational`, any number of them (RFC 9110 section 15.2); once their fields together
exceed `maxFieldSectionSize` (64 KiB) the request fails with `H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD`. Both callbacks run on the dispatcher of the coroutine that called `request`, never on the
connection's own single-threaded dispatcher, so a slow callback delays only its own request. There is no automatic
`100-continue`. `Http3Response.cancel()` (or cancelling the calling
coroutine) resets the stream with `H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED`; the connection keeps serving other requests.

### 0-RTT (opt-in, experimental)

`Http3Endpoint.connectEarly` resumes a ticket from an earlier connection and returns before the handshake completes
(ADR-0015). A request goes out in 0-RTT only when it sets `allowEarlyData = true` **and** is a safe method (GET, HEAD,
OPTIONS) without a body. Every other request waits for the handshake. If the server answers `425 Too Early`, the client
repeats the request once after the handshake (RFC 8470 section 5.2).

On the server, bind with `quicServerConfig(tls) { earlyData = true }`. The endpoint binds its SETTINGS into its tickets,
so changed SETTINGS refuse 0-RTT (RFC 9114 section 7.2.4.2). A request that arrived in 0-RTT before the handshake
completed is handled by `Http3Settings.earlyData`:

- `Http3EarlyDataPolicy.WaitForHandshake()` (the default): requests that `replayable` admits (GET, HEAD and OPTIONS by
  default) run at once with `receivedEarly = true`. Every other request reaches `acceptRequest()` only after the
  handshake completed. A replayed flight never completes the handshake, so a replayed unsafe request never runs.
- `Http3EarlyDataPolicy.Reject425()`: non-replayable early requests are answered with `425 Too Early` and never reach
  the application.

> **Replay warning.** An early request may be a copy an attacker sent again (RFC 9846 section 8). Handlers of requests
> that run early, those with `receivedEarly = true`, must have no side effects. Narrow `replayable` if a GET handler
> of yours changes state.

### Serving requests

```kotlin
// guide:http3:serve
val connection = server.accept()
while (true) {
    val request = connection.acceptRequest()
    launch {
        val writer = request.respond(200, Http3Headers.of("content-type" to "text/plain"))
        writer.output.writeStringUtf8("hello")
        writer.finish()                  // or finish(Http3Headers.of("x-checksum" to "...")) to send trailers
    }
}
```

Malformed requests never reach `acceptRequest`: their stream is reset with `H3_MESSAGE_ERROR` (that includes a
`content-length` that is not digits or conflicts with another; identical repeats collapse to one field). A response
field the validator rejects makes `respond` throw and resets the stream with `H3_INTERNAL_ERROR`. A request body the
application has not finished reading when its response is complete is dropped with `STOP_SENDING H3_NO_ERROR`; the
client's upload then ends with `QuicException.StreamError.Stopped` (code `H3_NO_ERROR`) in its body channel, and the
stream is retired as soon as the client's FIN or reset arrives, so unread uploads never exhaust the stream credit. Field
names and values are octets: a character above U+00FF is rejected rather than truncated. A response to HEAD may carry
a `content-length` without a body; the server drops whatever the application writes to a HEAD, 204 or 304 response
rather than sending DATA the client must treat as malformed. A request whose header
section is above `maxFieldSectionSize` once decoded is answered with 431 and `STOP_SENDING H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD` by the
connection itself. The other way round, a section above the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` is never sent:
`request` fails with `FieldSectionTooLarge` before it opens a stream, `respond` and `finish(trailers)` fail before
writing; refused trailers also reset the stream with `H3_INTERNAL_ERROR`, since the body already went out. Refused request
trailers reset the stream with `H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED`, and `request` (or, once the response began, its body and
`trailers`) fails with `FieldSectionTooLarge`. `request.remoteAddress` follows the client's path when it migrates.

### Shutdown and GOAWAY

`connection.goAway()` shuts a connection down gracefully (RFC 9114 section 5.2). A server first announces
2^62-4 ("no promises yet"), waits about two round trips so requests already in flight arrive, then announces the first
request id it will not process; such requests are reset with `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED`. Once every request below that id
is answered — including one whose HEADERS were still arriving when GOAWAY went out — and every response has been
acknowledged by the client's QUIC stack, the connection is closed with `H3_NO_ERROR`: by the client, which closes an
idle connection after a GOAWAY once its responses are read (a Kuicksilver client always does; quic-go's server waits for
exactly that), or by the server three seconds later if the client does not. A client that never closes (some other
stacks) therefore has three seconds to read a response its QUIC stack has acknowledged; data still unread then is lost
with the connection. A response handed to QUIC is not yet received, which is why the server waits for the client
rather than closing a fixed time after the last answer. A stream gets 10 seconds after the final GOAWAY to complete its HEADERS; after that it is reset with
`H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` (it was never processed) and no longer holds the connection open. (quic-go has no such
per-stream deadline; it bounds the whole graceful shutdown with the caller's context.) A client receiving GOAWAY fails the requests it did not cover, and every
new request, with `Http3Exception.RequestNotProcessed(retrySafe = true)`: they were never processed and can be sent
again on a new connection (the Ktor engine does that by itself). Once the requests and responses it still has are done
(bodies read, tunnels ended), a client that received GOAWAY closes the connection with `H3_NO_ERROR`. A client's own
`goAway()` sends GOAWAY(0) and stops issuing requests. `goAway()` may be called from any thread; it runs on the connection's own dispatcher.

`Http3Endpoint.close()` ends every connection at once, without GOAWAY, with `H3_NO_ERROR` (a QUIC endpoint's `close()`
sends application code 0, which HTTP/3 does not define); `Http3Endpoint.shutdown(grace)` is the graceful way.

A peer that keeps sending frames nobody needs (unknown frames on the control stream or on a request stream — reserved GREASE types on a request stream are free —
unidirectional streams that end or are reset before their type, PRIORITY_UPDATE floods) spends tokens of a glitch bucket (1000 tokens, 33 per second); an empty bucket closes the
connection with `H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD`. `Http3Settings.glitchProtection = false` turns this off.

### Priorities

Requests carry RFC 9218 priorities: `Http3Request.priority` becomes the `priority` field when it differs from the
default (`u=3`, not incremental), and `Http3Response.updatePriority(...)` sends a PRIORITY_UPDATE later. The client
schedules its own request stream with the same signal, whether it came as `Http3Request.priority` or as a `priority`
header. The server acts on the client's signal: `Http3ServerRequest.priority` follows the field and later updates, and
the response stream is scheduled with it unless the server picks its own, with `respond(status, headers, priority)` or
with a `priority` field in the response headers, which is merged into the stream's current priority (a parameter it
leaves out keeps that value: the client's, or an unsignalled tunnel's incremental default; RFC 9218 section 8, as h2o
does); the server's choice then stays. A CONNECT tunnel without a
signal is scheduled incremental on both sides (sections 10.1, 11), so a long-lived WebSocket shares bandwidth with the
responses next to it instead of holding them back; its client's signal itself still reads as the default. The
transport scheduler serves eight urgency levels in order and shares a level round-robin between incremental streams;
the control and QPACK streams always go first. A PRIORITY_UPDATE that arrives before its stream is remembered (up to 32
of them); one that arrives after the field replaces it.

### Extended CONNECT and datagrams

A server that accepts Extended CONNECT (RFC 9220) sets `enableConnectProtocol = true`; a client calls `connect`, which
waits for the server's SETTINGS and fails with `Http3Exception.Settings` if the server did not opt in. The result is an
`Http3Stream`: a byte stream both ways (WebSocket frames for `:protocol = websocket`, the protocol's own framing otherwise,
or capsules, see [Capsules](#capsules-experimental)) plus HTTP datagrams bound to the stream (RFC 9297). `Http3Stream.headers` holds the peer's fields: the CONNECT request's on
the server, the 2xx response's on the client (for example `sec-websocket-protocol`, RFC 9220 section 3). Each
direction ends on its own: closing `output` sends FIN and leaves `input` readable until the peer's FIN (a TCP-style
half-close, RFC 9114 section 4.4); the stream is released once both directions ended or the stream was reset. Datagrams
follow the stream's state (RFC 9297 section 2.1): the `datagrams` flow ends when the receive side closes and later
datagrams for the stream are dropped; once our send side is closed (`output` closed, or `reset`) `trySendDatagram`
answers `Closed` and `sendDatagram` throws `IllegalStateException`.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:connect (server)
val request = connection.acceptRequest()
if (request.protocol == "echo") {
    val stream = request.acceptConnect()          // :status 200
    stream.input.copyTo(stream.output)
} else request.respond(501).finish()

// guide:http3:connect (client)
val stream = client.connect(http3Request("CONNECT", "example.com", "/chat"), protocol = "echo")
stream.trySendDatagram(byteArrayOf(1, 2, 3))      // Unsupported until both sides sent SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM=1
stream.datagrams.collect { println(it.size) }
```

`SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM` is always sent (its absence would be a fingerprint); it is 1 only when the QUIC connection has
datagrams on. A peer that announces it without QUIC datagram support is a connection error `H3_SETTINGS_ERROR`.
Datagrams for streams nobody registered are dropped silently; a datagram whose quarter stream ID cannot be parsed
closes the connection with `H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR`. Each stream keeps the newest 32 datagrams nobody has collected.

#### Capsules (experimental)

Protocols such as WebTransport and CONNECT-UDP frame the stream's data as capsules (RFC 9297 section 3): a type, a
length and a value. `Http3Stream.useCapsuleProtocol(config)` turns a stream into a `CapsuleStream`; from then on the
stream's `input`, `output` and `datagrams` belong to it. `capsules` delivers the capsule types listed in
`CapsuleConfig.knownTypes` (64 KiB each at most by default) and skips every other type as its bytes arrive; `send`
writes one capsule whole, never interleaved with another; `close()` writes what is queued and then sends FIN, while
`capsules` keeps reading the peer's side.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:capsules (server)
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
val config = capsuleConfig { knownTypes = setOf(0x2843) }   // the capsule types the protocol defines
val tunnel = request.acceptConnect().useCapsuleProtocol(config)
tunnel.capsules.collect { tunnel.send(it) }                 // echo each capsule until the client's FIN
tunnel.close()                                              // the queued capsules, then FIN

// guide:http3:capsules (client)
val capsules = client.connect(http3Request("CONNECT", "example.com", "/chat"), protocol = "echo").useCapsuleProtocol(config)
capsules.send(Capsule(0x2843, "hello".encodeToByteArray()))
capsules.close()
val echoed = capsules.capsules.toList()                     // ends at the server's FIN
```

The stream is checked against RFC 9297 section 3.2 first: a peer message with `content-length`, `content-type` or
`transfer-encoding`, or a 204, 205 or 206 response, is malformed, so the stream is reset with `H3_MESSAGE_ERROR` and
`useCapsuleProtocol` throws `Http3Exception.MessageError`. The same happens later when the peer's FIN cuts a capsule in
two or a known capsule is longer than `maxCapsuleLength`: `capsules` fails with `MessageError` instead of ending, so a cut
stream is never mistaken for a clean end. A protocol whose last capsule closes the stream (WebTransport's
WT_CLOSE_SESSION) lists it in `terminalTypes`: the capsule is delivered, and anything after it is malformed the same way.
The connection lives on in every case.

Datagrams work as on a plain stream, plus DATAGRAM capsules (RFC 9297 section 3.5): those the peer sends arrive in
`datagrams` together with QUIC datagrams, and a DATAGRAM capsule longer than `maxDatagramLength` is dropped unread. When
HTTP/3 datagrams are unsupported on the connection (either side's `SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM` is 0), `trySendDatagram` and
`sendDatagram` send a DATAGRAM capsule instead, unless `datagramFallback = false` (until the peer's SETTINGS arrive,
datagrams count as unsupported); a datagram too large for a QUIC
DATAGRAM frame is answered `TooLarge`, not sent as a capsule. `CapsuleProtocol.isEnabled(headers)` reads the
`Capsule-Protocol` header field (section 3.4) and `CapsuleProtocol.Enabled` writes it; the stream does not require it.

Reading pauses while `receiveQueue` capsules (16) wait for the collector, which holds the peer back through flow control,
so collect `capsules` even when only datagrams matter, or list no `knownTypes`. `send`, `close()` and a falling-back
`sendDatagram` have no deadline of their own while the peer withholds flow-control credit; cancelling `close()` leaves
the writer running in the connection, so bound them with `withTimeout` and `reset` the stream when it expires. Options:
[configuration reference](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/configuration.md#capsuleconfig-experimental). The Capsule Protocol is only available on HTTP/3;
HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 upgrades are not supported.

### WebTransport (experimental)

WebTransport over HTTP/3 (draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-16) is experimental (`@ExperimentalKuicksilverApi`): sessions,
their streams and datagrams, close and drain. Both sides set `webTransport = true` in `http3Settings` (it needs
`enableConnectProtocol` and `h3Datagram`; `Http3Endpoint.bind` refuses it when QUIC datagrams are off). Browsers do not
speak draft-16 yet, so a server announces the SETTINGS of draft-02 (Chrome, Firefox) and draft-14 (Safari) too and
accepts both `:protocol` tokens, `webtransport-h3` and `webtransport`; a client picks the token from the server's
SETTINGS. A request with either token is `isWebTransport`; `acceptWebTransport` answers 200 once the client's SETTINGS
arrived (ten seconds at most; without them, or without HTTP datagrams, the request is answered with 400 and
`acceptWebTransport` throws `Http3Exception.Settings`), and a 4xx from `respond` refuses the session. The client waits
ten seconds for the server's SETTINGS and ten more for the answer to its CONNECT (`WebTransportException.Timeout`). Check the `origin` field before accepting a browser's session. The client offers application
protocols in `WT-Available-Protocols` and the server picks one of `availableProtocols`; a choice the client did not
offer fails `webTransport` with `WebTransportException.Alpn` (a `WT-Protocol` that is not a valid Structured Field
String is ignored).

There is no WebTransport flow control, so a connection carries one session: a client refuses a second one with
`IllegalStateException`, a server resets a second CONNECT with `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` before the application sees it.
WebTransport streams that arrive before their session was accepted wait, 16 per connection for up to 5 s each; the
others are rejected with `WT_BUFFERED_STREAM_REJECTED`.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:webtransport (server)
val request = connection.acceptRequest()
if (request.isWebTransport && request.headers["origin"] == "https://app.example") {
    val session = request.acceptWebTransport(protocol = request.availableProtocols.firstOrNull())
} else request.respond(403).finish()

// guide:http3:webtransport (client)
val request = http3Request("CONNECT", "example.com", "/wt") { headers = Http3Headers.of("origin" to "https://app.example") }
val session = client.webTransport(request, protocols = listOf("chat-v1"))
println(session.protocol)                          // "chat-v1" when the server chose it
```

A session opens and accepts streams (`openBidi`, `openUni`, `acceptBidi`, `acceptUni`) whose `input` and `output`
are plain byte channels, and sends and receives datagrams (`trySendDatagram`, `sendDatagram`, `receiveDatagram`, the
newest 32 kept), which may be lost like any QUIC datagram. Application error codes are 0..2^32-1, for streams
(`reset`, `stopSending`, reported as `WebTransportException.StreamReset` and `StreamStopped`) and for the session;
on the wire they travel mapped into the HTTP/3 code space (section 4.4). `close(code, reason)` sends
WT_CLOSE_SESSION (the reason cut to 1024 bytes of UTF-8), then FIN, and waits for the peer's FIN (stopping the peer
after five seconds without it); either side's close,
the peer's FIN or a failure completes `closed` with the code, the reason or the cause, resets the session's streams
with `WT_SESSION_GONE`, and frees the connection for a next session. `drain()` asks the peer to wind down;
`drainRequested` turns true on the peer's request, an HTTP/3 GOAWAY, or this side's own `drain()` (the side that asks
winds down too, draft-ietf-webtrans-http3 section 4.7). Writing the close waits at most five seconds
for the peer's flow-control credit; opening a stream waits for the peer's stream credit without a deadline, so bound
it with `withTimeout`. WebTransport's own flow control (`WT_MAX_DATA` and the like) is not implemented: those capsules
are ignored, and the QUIC limits (`maxBidiStreams`, `maxUniStreams`, the stream and connection windows) bound a
session. With `QuicConfig.resetStreamAt` on both sides a stream we opened is reset with RESET_STREAM_AT, which keeps its header
so the peer can still tell its session (section 4.4); without it the reset is a plain RESET_STREAM. The Ktor server turns
it on with `webTransport`.

```kotlin
// guide:http3:webtransport-echo (server)
val stream = session.acceptBidi()                 // the client's stream
stream.input.copyTo(stream.output)                // echo until its FIN
stream.output.flushAndClose()
session.sendDatagram(session.receiveDatagram())   // and one datagram back
println(session.closed.await().reason)            // "done" once the client closed

// guide:http3:webtransport-echo (client)
val stream = session.openBidi()
stream.output.writeFully("ping".encodeToByteArray())
stream.output.flushAndClose()
println(stream.input.readBuffer().readString())  // "ping"
session.trySendDatagram(byteArrayOf(1, 2, 3))
println(session.receiveDatagram().size)
session.close(0, "done")
```

## Ktor engines

Kuicksilver plugs into Ktor 3.6 as a server engine (`io.kuicksilver:kuicksilver-ktor-server`) and a client engine
(`io.kuicksilver:kuicksilver-ktor-client`). Both speak HTTP/1.1 over TLS 1.3 (`kuicksilver-ktor-network`) and HTTP/3
(`kuicksilver-http3`); both also speak HTTP/2 over TLS (`kuicksilver-http2`, ADR-0017), opt-in on the server ([HTTP/2 on the server](#http2-on-the-server)). The code blocks below compile and run as `GuideSamplesTest`
(`kuicksilver-ktor-server/src/jvmTest` and `kuicksilver-ktor-client/src/jvmTest`); the engines' other tests run on every
target (see "Compatibility"). Every engine option with its default is in the [configuration
reference](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/configuration.md); common failures are in [troubleshooting](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/troubleshooting.md).

### Server

```kotlin
// guide:ktor:server
val server = embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, configure = {
    tlsConnector(TlsIdentity.fromPem(chainPem, keyPem.toCharArray())) {   // the key array is zeroed after import
        port = 443
        clientAuth = ClientAuth.Optional              // ask for a client certificate without requiring one
        trust = TrustConfig.AnchoredCa(listOf(clientCa))
    }
}) {
    routing {
        get("/") { call.respondText("hello, ${call.request.peerCertificates.size} certificates") }
    }
}
server.start(wait = true)
```

- A `tlsConnector` serves HTTP/1.1 over TLS on TCP; Ktor's HTTP/1.1 parser (`ktor-http-cio`) and a copy of the CIO
  engine's connection pipeline handle requests, so keep-alive, pipelining, chunked bodies and `100-continue` behave as
  in the CIO engine. Request framing follows RFC 9112 section 6 more strictly than CIO: a request with both
  Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding is refused with 400 and the connection closed, a request with neither has no
  body (also with `Connection: close`), and a chunked trailer section is accepted (its fields are discarded). A
  chunk-size line must follow RFC 9112 section 7.1 exactly (hex digits, extensions by their grammar, no whitespace
  right before the CRLF, which 0.2.0 and Go's net/http tolerate): anything else, such as a bare CR or LF in it, makes the handler's receive of the body fail with
  `BadRequestException` (Ktor answers 400 unless the application handles it) and the connection closes. An HTTP/1.1
  request without a Host field, or any request with two, gets 400 and the connection closed (RFC 9112 section 3.2).
  The engine cannot act as a CONNECT proxy yet (planned for 0.3.0): a CONNECT reaches the application, but a 2xx answer
  goes out as `501 Not Implemented` with a warning in the application log, since a 2xx would promise a tunnel; every
  CONNECT ends its connection (RFC 9931 section 8). The engine's own 400 has the fixed body `Bad Request`
  (Ktor CIO sends the parser's message, which can quote the request's header fields). ALPN on TCP is `http/1.1`.
- `configuration.identity = ...` turns plain connectors into TLS ones, so `embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, port = 443,
  configure = { identity = ... })` works as expected. Without an identity a plain `connector { port = ... }` serves
  cleartext HTTP/1.1 (behind a TLS-terminating proxy, for tests).
- On the JVM, Ktor's `sslConnector(keyStore, alias, ...) {}` (and the `ktor.security.ssl.*` keys) is accepted: the key
  and chain under the alias become the identity, and a trust store makes client certificates required, as in Ktor's
  Netty and Jetty engines. Any other HTTPS connector type fails with `TlsException.Config` rather than serving cleartext.
- `call.request.peerCertificates` is the client certificate chain as the TLS layer validated it (empty without client
  authentication). Ktor has no equivalent.
- Slow and silent clients (slowloris): a client has `requestHeaderTimeoutSeconds` (*experimental*, 30 s) to send a
  complete request head, counted from the accepted TCP connection for the first request (the TLS handshake included)
  and from the end of the previous response on a keep-alive connection; header bytes trickling in do not extend it. One
  that sent part of a head by then gets `408 Request Timeout` with `Connection: close`; one that sent nothing (or never
  finished the TLS handshake) is closed without a response. `connectionIdleTimeoutSeconds` (45 s) closes a connection
  without requests in both directions, and a request body that sends no byte for that long gets `408 Request Timeout`
  and ends the connection, unless the application or StatusPages answers the failed read itself (a slow but moving
  upload is read in full; after `Expect: 100-continue` the wait starts once `100 Continue` is sent). A body the handler
  leaves unread is dropped up to 256 KiB; a larger rest, a chunked one still incomplete when the response starts, or a
  request answered without the `100 Continue` it asked for, ends the connection after a response that says
  `Connection: close`. One whose client stopped reading its response (the socket took nothing) is closed after the
  longer of that and 5 minutes: the engine sees progress about 1 MiB at a time, and 5 minutes serve
  clients down to about 3.4 KiB/s. A closing connection sends what is left for as long as the client takes it, and is
  aborted after the same deadline without progress, so a slow reader's last response is not cut short.
  Empty lines before a request line are skipped and do not count as a started request. A request head (request line
  and header fields) above 64 KiB, the HTTP/3 default `maxFieldSectionSize`, gets `431 Request Header Fields Too
  Large` and the connection closes; a single line above 8 KiB gets 400. A failing `accept()` (the descriptor table
  full: EMFILE, ENFILE) is retried after 5 ms, doubling up to 1 s, instead of at once, and logged at most once per
  10 s with the number of failures left out. How many connections a connector holds, in all and per client address,
  is bounded too: [Connection limits](#connection-limits).
- A TLS handshake failure closes only that connection. `resolvedConnectors()` reports the real ports when you bind port
  0; `stop(grace, timeout)` stops accepting, sends GOAWAY to every HTTP/3 connection at once, raises `ApplicationStopPreparing`
  and waits for running calls (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/3) until the grace period, then cuts what is left at the timeout.
- Optional whitespace around a response header value is trimmed before the value goes out over HTTP/3 (field values
  carry none); a value HTTP/3 cannot carry (a character above U+00FF, or a control character other than tab) fails the call and resets its stream.

#### Connection limits

Each TCP connector holds at most `maxTcpConnections` (*experimental*, 10,000) connections at once, and, when it is set,
at most `maxTcpConnectionsPerIp` (*experimental*, off by default) from one client address, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 alike. A
connection counts from `accept` (its TLS handshake included) until its socket is released (a socket whose release hangs
is given up after the abort wait, so for that moment the descriptors in use can briefly exceed the limit).

- At `maxTcpConnections` the connector stops accepting, as Go's `netutil.LimitListener`, Jetty's `ConnectionLimit` and
  nginx's `worker_connections` do: new clients wait in the OS backlog (their connect succeeds, nothing is read from
  them) and are accepted as connections close; the server spends no descriptor or TLS work on them. Once the backlog is
  full too (511 on the JVM, 50 on Kotlin/Native), the OS drops further connection attempts (Linux by default, with
  `tcp_abort_on_overflow` 0: the client's TCP retries its SYN) or resets them. Waiting clients are not reported to the
  event listener.
- `maxTcpConnectionsPerIp` is off by default, as in nginx, Caddy, Go, Jetty, Netty, Envoy and HAProxy. Behind a reverse
  proxy, a load balancer, Kubernetes source NAT or any NAT every client shares one address, and an HTTP/1.1 proxy opens
  an upstream connection per request in flight (plus one per WebSocket or SSE stream). Enable it (256, say) only when
  the server faces its clients directly. Over it, a connection is reset right after `accept`, before its TLS handshake
  (an address is known only then), as nginx's stream `limit_conn` and Envoy's `connection_limit` filter do; a proxy in
  front reports that as 502 or 503, and its passive health checks may take the server out.
  `KuicksilverServerEventListener.connectionRefused` hears it with the reason `per-IP limit`; the application log gets
  one warning, then at most one per 10 s with a count. An address is its bytes, never looked up as a name: an
  IPv4-mapped client counts as its IPv4 address, an IPv6 client by its whole address, as QUIC's `maxConnectionsPerIp`
  counts HTTP/3 clients, so a client that holds a /64 gets around it.
- The checks run cheapest first: the connection slot before `accept`, the per-address count right after it, then
  `http2RepeatOffenderPenalty` (when on), and only then the TLS handshake.
- The default 10,000 does not protect a process whose descriptor limit is lower (`ulimit -n`: 256 in a macOS shell,
  often 1024 on Linux): raise that limit, or set `maxTcpConnections` below it, leaving room for the UDP sockets, files
  and outgoing connections the application opens. Above it `accept()` fails with EMFILE; the engine then backs off
  (5 ms doubling to 1 s) instead of spinning, but clients wait until descriptors free up.
- `EngineMain` keys `kuicksilver.maxTcpConnections` and `kuicksilver.maxTcpConnectionsPerIp` (`0` or absent is off).
- HTTP/3 has its own limits in the QUIC endpoint, `maxConnections` and `maxConnectionsPerIp` (the same 10,000 and 256),
  which the engine does not let you change yet ([deployment guide](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/deployment.md#security-limits)).

#### HTTP/3 on the server

Every TLS connector also serves HTTP/3 on UDP on the same port number; the two sockets are bound as a pair, so with
`port = 0` both share the resolved port (`resolvedConnectors()` lists the TCP connectors). The OS
picks the TCP port first, so its UDP twin may be taken: the pair is then bound again on a new port, up to 16 times,
every other time with the UDP port picked first and TCP taking the same number, after which the connector serves
HTTP/1.1 alone with a warning. A fixed port whose UDP side is taken fails the start. HTTP/1.1
responses then carry `Alt-Svc: h3=":<port>"; ma=86400` so clients can switch (RFC 7838) — unless the application set
its own `Alt-Svc`, or the response is a 421; `altSvc = false` turns the header off.

In an HTTP/3 call `call.request.httpVersion` is `"HTTP/3"`, `call.request.local.scheme` is the request's `:scheme`
(`"https"` from browsers and the Kuicksilver client; `"http"` when a client sends that), `serverPort` without a port in
`:authority` is that scheme's default (80 or 443), the `:authority` appears as the `Host` header, and `call.request.local.remoteAddress` follows the client when it migrates to another
network. Responses never carry `Transfer-Encoding` or other connection-specific headers: bodies of unknown length are
simply a sequence of DATA frames.

Knobs, named after Ktor's Netty engine where one exists: `http3` (on), `quic` (transport settings), `quicMaxIdleTimeout`
(applies while `quic` is not assigned), `udpSocketCount` (endpoint loops on the UDP port, every platform with a QUIC server), `quicAdmission`
(Retry policy, Ktor-Netty's `quicTokenHandler`), `quicLoadBalancer` (QUIC-LB connection IDs, experimental;
`engine.updateLoadBalancer` changes them, [QUIC: Behind a load balancer](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/quic.md#behind-a-load-balancer)), `http3Settings`. UDP socket buffer sizes are not configurable yet.

The engine serves HTTP/3 on every target, Kotlin/Native Linux, Apple and Windows included (the accelerated `ksl` socket,
ADR-0006); `udpSocketCount > 1` works wherever HTTP/3 does: a socket per loop with `SO_REUSEPORT` on Linux and Android,
one socket routed by connection ID in process on macOS, iOS and Windows ([QUIC: Several loops on one port](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/quic.md#several-loops-on-one-port)).
Where a QUIC server cannot run, the engine logs a warning and serves
HTTP/1.1 only, without `Alt-Svc`. The same applies to a `tlsConnector` with a `sniSelector`: QUIC cannot pick an
identity per SNI name (not supported for QUIC yet), so that connector skips HTTP/3 with a warning instead of failing to start.

Running it in production (UDP in firewalls, Docker and Kubernetes, load balancers, kernel buffers, checking that clients
arrive over HTTP/3): [Deploying the HTTP/3 server](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/deployment.md).

#### HTTP/2 on the server

`http2 = true` (experimental; off by default in 0.3.0; `EngineMain` key `kuicksilver.http2`) makes every TLS connector
offer `h2` before `http/1.1` in ALPN, so a client that offers both gets HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) and one that offers only
`http/1.1` (WebSockets included) gets HTTP/1.1 on the same port, as before. Plain connectors never serve HTTP/2: there
is no h2c, and a client's `PRI * HTTP/2.0` preface is refused with `505 HTTP Version Not Supported`. HTTP/2 runs over
TLS 1.3 only, which is all the server engine negotiates (RFC 9113 section 9.2).

```kotlin
// guide:ktor:http2-server
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
val server = embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, configure = {
    tlsConnector(identity) { port = 443 }
    http2 = true                                              // offer h2 before http/1.1 in ALPN
    http2Settings = Http2Settings(maxConcurrentStreams = 50)  // windows and flood limits are Http2Settings'
}, module = Application::module)
```

Each stream is a Ktor call: `call.request.httpVersion` is `"HTTP/2"`, `call.request.local.scheme` is `"https"` (the
connection's, whatever the request's `:scheme`), `:authority` appears as the `Host` header and split `cookie` fields as one (RFC 9113 section 8.2.3). Responses
go out without connection-specific headers (`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Upgrade` are dropped), a
response to HEAD, a 204 or a 304 without content, and every response carries the engine's `Alt-Svc` as on HTTP/1.1, so
a client on HTTP/2 learns HTTP/3 too. Requests are checked against RFC 9113 section 8 before the application sees them:
a malformed one (an uppercase or invalid field name, a connection-specific field, `te` other than `trailers`, a missing,
repeated or unknown pseudo-header field, `host` that differs from `:authority`, content that does not match
`content-length`) is reset with PROTOCOL_ERROR and the connection goes on; a field section above `maxHeaderListSize` is
answered 431. A CONNECT is answered 501 (the engine has no tunnels). WebSockets over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) are not offered:
the engine never sends SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL, so a request with `:protocol` is malformed. A request with
`Expect: 100-continue` gets an interim 100 when the handler first reads the body. Content that does not match the
response's `Content-Length` is never sent as a complete response (the stream is reset); a 1xx as the final status goes
out as a 500. A call that ends without a response resets its stream; one stream's failure (a client's reset, a handler's
exception) never affects the others on the connection.

`http2Settings` (`Http2Settings`) holds the windows, SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (100) and the field-section and
flood limits of the core ([configuration reference](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/configuration.md#ktor-server-engine)). The engine's deadlines apply:
the client's connection preface must arrive within `requestHeaderTimeoutSeconds` of the accepted connection (TLS
included), else GOAWAY and close; each field block must arrive within it too (else GOAWAY with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM); a
request body that sends no byte for `connectionIdleTimeoutSeconds` fails the handler's read and is answered 408 when
nothing else answered; a connection without requests for `connectionIdleTimeoutSeconds` gets GOAWAY and closes; a
response that gets no window from the client for the longer of that and 5 minutes resets its stream. Request content is
credited to the client only as the handler reads it. A client's RST_STREAM cancels the handler of that request; a
request still arriving when its handler is done with a complete response is stopped with RST_STREAM NO_ERROR (RFC 9113
section 8.1). `eventListener` reports these connections and calls with `HTTP_2_0`.

Flood defences (threat model, section 3.23): each connection is held to the core's limits (`http2Settings`: the reset
budget against Rapid Reset, the glitch budget against MadeYouReset and PING, SETTINGS or PRIORITY floods, 8 CONTINUATION
frames per field block, 10 000 queued control frames), and a broken limit ends it with GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM. A
stream the client reset cancels its handler and counts toward SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS until the handler
returns, so no more handlers run at once than that limit. A connection that is over gets what it still has to write
sent for as long as the client takes it; after the send-stall deadline without progress its socket is aborted (3
seconds when it ended in an error, such as a broken flood limit: only its GOAWAY is left to deliver). These
per-connection limits are the defence by default.

`http2RepeatOffenderPenalty` (experimental, `EngineMain` key `kuicksilver.http2RepeatOffenderPenalty`, e.g. `30s`; off
by default) adds a backoff by address: one whose HTTP/2 connections end in a flood limit's ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM three
times within a minute has its TCP connections (HTTP/1.1 too) closed at accept, before the TLS handshake, for that long,
with a warning logged at most every 10 seconds per connector. An IPv4 client counts by its address (also when a
dual-stack listener reports it as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`), an IPv6 client by its /56; a slow field block is no strike. Turn it
on only where the server sees each client's real address (directly exposed, or behind an L4 load balancer that keeps
the source address). Never behind a NAT, CGNAT, an L4 load balancer or Kubernetes Service that rewrites source
addresses (`externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`) or a TCP proxy such as HAProxy in TCP mode: every client there shares one
address, and one flooder would lock them all out.

The server passes h2spec 2.6.0 (all 146 cases, `tools/interop/h2spec.sh`). HTTP/2 on the server is still experimental and off by default in 0.3.0.

#### Turning HTTP/3 off on the server

A running server can stop advertising HTTP/3, or take it out of service, without a restart: set
`engine.http3Advertising` (experimental) from wherever your remote configuration arrives — a config poll, an admin
endpoint, a feature flag.

```kotlin
// guide:ktor:http3-advertising
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
val server = embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, configure = {
    tlsConnector(identity) { port = 443 }
}, module = Application::module)
// later, when the remote configuration says so: clients fall back to HTTP/1.1 over TLS
server.engine.http3Advertising = Http3Advertising.Drain
// and when the incident is over
server.engine.http3Advertising = Http3Advertising.On
```

| Value | HTTP/1.1 responses | HTTP/3 responses | Live HTTP/3 connections | New QUIC connections |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `On` (default) | `Alt-Svc: h3=":<port>"; ma=86400` | no `Alt-Svc` | served | accepted |
| `Clear` | `Alt-Svc: clear` | `Alt-Svc: clear` | served | accepted |
| `Drain` | `Alt-Svc: clear` | `Alt-Svc: clear` | GOAWAY (RFC 9114 section 5.2): requests in flight finish, then the connection closes | refused at the first Initial with CONNECTION_REFUSED |

RFC 7838 section 3: "A field value containing the special value "clear" indicates that the origin requests all
alternatives for that origin to be invalidated". An HTTP/3 response may send it too, since section 2.2 says
"Alternative services are fully authoritative for the origin in question, including the ability to clear or update
cached alternative service entries".

- Every response reads the value as its head goes out, so the next response on a keep-alive connection follows a
  change; every new client Initial is checked when the QUIC endpoint admits it. The setter returns at once.
- The header part applies where the engine sends `Alt-Svc` at all: on a TLS connector that serves HTTP/3, with
  `altSvc = true`. With `altSvc = false` no `Alt-Svc` is sent in any mode, but `Drain` still sends GOAWAY and refuses new
  QUIC connections. An `Alt-Svc` the application sets itself is left as it is in every mode, and a 421 gets none.
- `Clear` stops the advertising and withdraws it: a client drops the alternative at its next response, over HTTP/1.1 or
  HTTP/3. A connection it already has may go on serving it (RFC 7838 section 2.2 lets a client keep using one); to move
  those connections to TCP, use `Drain`.
- `Drain` sends GOAWAY to every live HTTP/3 connection at once, as a [graceful stop](#graceful-stop) does, and to every
  connection whose handshake completes while it is set. The requests in flight complete; once the last response is
  acknowledged the client closes the connection (a Kuicksilver client does), or the server three seconds later.
  **Not bounded in 0.3.0:** `Drain` has no grace deadline, so a long-lived stream (a WebSocket or WebTransport session
  over HTTP/3) keeps its connection until the application or the client ends it; a drain deadline is planned for 0.3.x.
  To cut such sessions, stop the server (its grace period applies) or end them in the application.
- A new client is refused with a stateless Initial CONNECTION_CLOSE carrying CONNECTION_REFUSED, as RFC 9000 section
  5.2.2 asks: "If a server refuses to accept a new connection, it SHOULD send an Initial packet containing a
  CONNECTION_CLOSE frame with error code CONNECTION_REFUSED" (sections 10.2.3 and 20.1). It is under the endpoint's
  stateless rate limit, runs before `quicAdmission` (which is not asked), unless a hard limit (`maxConnections`,
  `maxConnectionsPerIp`) drops the Initial first, and `EndpointStats.connectionsRefusedAdmission` counts it. A refused client falls back to TCP at once instead of waiting for
  its handshake timeout, and its next HTTP/1.1 response clears its cached alternative. A Kuicksilver client does not
  mark the alternative broken for the refusal ([Racing and fallback](#racing-and-fallback)), so once the instance (or
  another one) serves HTTP/3 and announces it again, the client is back on HTTP/3 with its next call.
- The UDP socket stays bound under `Drain`: releasing the port and binding it again on `On` would race other processes
  for it (and, with `udpSocketCount > 1` on Linux and Android, for each of its sockets), and a closed port answers with nothing or an ICMP
  error that clients only notice at their handshake timeout. To block UDP outright, use the firewall.
- Back to `On` (or `Clear`), new QUIC connections are accepted again. GOAWAY cannot be taken back (RFC 9114 section 5.2),
  so connections drained before keep closing; their clients open new ones.
- The value is per engine and is not kept across restarts: a new engine starts at `On`. Behind a load balancer set it on
  every instance.

#### WebSockets over HTTP/3

With `webSocketsOverHttp3 = true` (the default) the HTTP/3 listener advertises `SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL` and
accepts Extended CONNECT with `:protocol = websocket` (RFC 9220). Such a request reaches Ktor's pipeline as the HTTP/1.1
upgrade request the `WebSockets` plugin knows — `GET` with `Connection: Upgrade`, `Upgrade: websocket` and a
`Sec-WebSocket-Key` — so ordinary `webSocket("/path") {}` routes serve it unchanged; the upgrade is answered with
`:status 200` and the frames travel on the request stream. Extended CONNECT with any other protocol is answered 501 (WebTransport aside when it is on, below). A
plain HTTP/1.1 `Upgrade` on an HTTP/3 request is meaningless (RFC 9114 section 4.5) and gets 501 too.

#### WebTransport over HTTP/3 (experimental)

With `webTransport = true` the HTTP/3 listener speaks WebTransport (draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-16, plus the SETTINGS of
draft-02 and draft-14 that browsers send; see the [HTTP/3 guide](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/http3.md#webtransport-experimental)), and a
`webTransport("/path") { session -> }` route serves the sessions. It matches only a WebTransport Extended CONNECT over
HTTP/3, never an HTTP/1.1 request (a request of another method to the path gets Ktor's 405); a WebTransport request
no route matches gets Ktor's 404, and one that another route answers with a 2xx gets 501 instead, since no session
was accepted. The route checks the
`origin` field first: `checkOrigin` refuses with 403, and its default, `sameHostOrigin`, admits the server's own
origin and clients that send none (browsers always send one; pass your own check for a page served elsewhere). The
server picks the first of the route's `protocols` the client offers. Then the session is accepted and the handler
runs; when it returns the session is closed with code 0, when it throws with `WEB_TRANSPORT_HANDLER_FAILED` (1) and
an empty reason. One session per connection: there is no WebTransport flow control yet.

```kotlin
// guide:ktor:webtransport-server
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
val server = embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, configure = {
    tlsConnector(identity) { port = 443 }
    webTransport = true
}) {
    routing {
        webTransport("/echo", protocols = listOf("echo-v1")) { session ->
            val stream = session.acceptBidi()
            stream.input.copyTo(stream.output)
            stream.output.flushAndClose()
        }                                          // returning closes the session with code 0
    }
}
```

A real browser is checked by `ChromeWebTransportTest` (`kuicksilver-ktor-server` jvmTest), which runs only on request
and only with an installed Chrome or Chromium:

```sh
./gradlew :kuicksilver-ktor-server:jvmTest --tests '*ChromeWebTransportTest*' -Pkuicksilver.browserTests=true
```

It starts Chrome headless with a throw-away profile, QUIC forced for the test origin and the test certificate admitted
by its SPKI hash, and the page `wt/index.html` from the test resources posts its results back. Firefox is checked by
hand with one command:

```sh
tools/interop/wt-firefox-manual.sh
```

It makes a P-256 certificate valid for 13 days (browsers pin only a certificate valid for at most 14 days and not RSA
by hash) and its SHA-256 hash, starts `ManualWebTransportServer` (`kuicksilver-ktor-server` jvmTest, opt-in with
`-Pkuicksilver.manualWebTransport=true`) with that page and the test's two routes on `127.0.0.1`, and opens
`https://localhost:<port>/wt/index.html?hash=<b64>` in Firefox with a throw-away profile. Accept Firefox's certificate
warning for the page once (`serverCertificateHashes` only covers the WebTransport sessions); the script then prints
PASS or FAIL with the page's JSON and stops Firefox and the server (variables in the script's header). On FAIL it keeps
its temporary directory and lists it: `server-events.txt` (how each session and connection ended, with the cause),
the server's qlog, Firefox's own qlog and MOZ_LOG. To check Safari
by hand, start the same server with a certificate such as `openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt
ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -days 13 -nodes -subj /CN=localhost -addext subjectAltName=DNS:localhost -keyout wt.key -out
wt.pem` (OpenSSL 3, which writes the PKCS#8 key the server reads): `./gradlew :kuicksilver-ktor-server:jvmTest --tests
'*ManualWebTransportServer*' -Pkuicksilver.manualWebTransport=true -Pkuicksilver.manualWebTransport.cert=$PWD/wt.pem
-Pkuicksilver.manualWebTransport.key=$PWD/wt.key -Pkuicksilver.manualWebTransport.port=<port>`, open
`https://localhost:<port>/wt/index.html?hash=<b64>` with `<b64>` from `openssl x509 -in wt.pem -outform der | openssl
dgst -sha256 -binary | base64` (percent-encoded in the URL) and accept the certificate warning for the page; each step
prints `ok` on the page and the Gradle run passes once the page has posted its result. Record the result in
`docs/spec/interop.md`, "Interop WebTransport".

#### Certificate rotation

A renewed certificate can be put in place without a restart (experimental). Give the connector a
`TlsIdentity.Reloadable` and call `reload` when the new files are there (from a deploy hook, an admin route, a timer):

```kotlin
// guide:ktor:certificate-rotation
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalKuicksilverApi::class)   // experimental API (at the top of the file)
val identity = TlsIdentity.reloadable(TlsIdentity.fromPem(chainPem, keyChars)) // the key array is zeroed after import
val server = embeddedServer(Kuicksilver, configure = {
    tlsConnector(identity) { port = 443 }
}, module = Application::module)
// later, when the renewed files are in place: new TCP and QUIC handshakes present them, open connections keep theirs
identity.reload(TlsIdentity.fromPem(renewedChainPem, renewedKeyChars))
```

`keyChars` and `renewedKeyChars` are the key files read into `CharArray`s (not through a `String`, which would leave the
key on the heap). Every handshake that starts after `reload` returns, HTTP/1.1 over TCP and HTTP/3 over QUIC, presents
the new chain and key; handshakes in progress and open connections keep the old ones. A key that does not match its
certificate fails in `fromPem`, and `reload` refuses an expired leaf and one not valid yet (`TlsException.Config`): the
identity in use stays. Session tickets are bound to the certificate they were issued under, so after a reload clients
run one full handshake and see the new certificate (see [Rotating the server certificate](https://github.com/kuicksilver/kuicksilver/blob/main/docs/guide/tls.md#rotating-the-server-certificate)
for ownership, resumption and key compromise). The same works for `identity` in the engine configuration (plain
connectors served over TLS); on the JVM, an `sslConnector` keystore is read once, so build the identity with
`TlsIdentity.fromKeyStore` and wrap it yourself instead.

With `EngineMain`, set `kuicksilver.tls.reloadInterval` (`1h`, `30m`, ...; off by default) and the engine checks the
PEM files of `kuicksilver.tls.certificateChain` and `kuicksilver.tls.privateKey` that often (the configuration's
`identityReloadInterval`). It reloads when the chain file holds other certificates than those served: a chain read
twice a second apart with the same content, and a key that matches it. Tools that write the chain before the key
(certbot) or swap a symlinked directory (Kubernetes secrets) are covered: a pair that does not match yet keeps the old
identity and is tried again after 1 s, then 2 s, 4 s and so on up to the interval. Failures are logged as warnings
(once per distinct failure, never with key material); a successful reload is logged at info level, and the files are
read once more a second later, so a chain whose writer paused longer than that is corrected then. Each file is read
whole on every check and refused above 1 MiB; a chain file that also holds a private key is refused, at startup too (keep
the key in its own file). The stop waits at most a second for a check in progress (a read on a hung network file system
cannot be interrupted). Polling once an hour means a renewed certificate may wait an hour to be served; certbot's `--deploy-hook`
(or a restart) is the alternative when it must take effect at once. With `kuicksilver.tls.reloadInterval` set, the
files at startup get the same checks as a reload, so an expired or not yet valid certificate fails the start; without
it, `EngineMain` serves the files as they are, as before. The identity `EngineMain` made is closed when the server stops.

#### EngineMain and configuration keys

`io.kuicksilver.ktor.server.EngineMain` reads the usual `ktor.deployment.*` keys (and on the JVM `-sslPort` with
`ktor.security.ssl.*`). Its own keys work on every platform:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kuicksilver.tls.certificateChain`, `kuicksilver.tls.privateKey` | PEM files; the deployment port then serves TLS and HTTP/3 |
